dailyRead: Today is a correction day, and two of the corrections matter more than anything new that printed. The first is the yen. Yesterday's file said the BoJ was roughly 87% priced for September 18 and concluded that the Bank of Japan was better priced than the Fed, which was the load-bearing leg of the USD/JPY short. Checked against rate markets this morning, that number is wrong: OIS-derived pricing puts a 25bp move to 1.25% at 57%, and the softer trader-sentiment measures sit near 80%, while the Fed has moved ABOVE 65% on CME FedWatch, up from 57-60% yesterday and 36% before Warsh spoke. The comparison is therefore inverted, not merely narrower. That is why JPY is downgraded from +1 to 0 and why USD/JPY goes from SHORT to RANGE rather than flipping to LONG. The pair is 159.968, up 0.14% today and 0.48% on the week, sitting on the line both capitals have defended since the July 31 joint intervention, and it has now spent three sessions there without a response. The intervention record argues for caution on both sides: the Ministry of Finance spent a record 11.73 trillion yen across April and May after 160 broke and bought roughly six weeks before the trend reasserted itself, and the late-July operation has already been fully retraced. Selling the yen into that setup is not a trade with a good risk profile even though the rate differential now favours it, so the honest answer is a range with LOW conviction and an explicit instruction not to chase above 160. What supports the yen underneath is real but not yet price-relevant: Q2 capital spending printed +1.6% y/y against a 0.2% consensus, Tokyo CPI ex food and energy is 2.0%, the jobless rate is 2.4% at a one-year low, retail sales are +4.0% y/y and Himino has said the Bank will consider a hike at every meeting including September. The second correction is sterling. Yesterday's downgrade to zero rested explicitly on UK hike expectations being cut further and pushed to November at the earliest. The evidence says the opposite. The 10-year gilt is 5.2077%, the highest yield in the G10 and up 26 basis points on the month, LSEG data shows markets pricing 24 basis points of BoE tightening by December and 36 basis points by February 2027, and BRC shop-price inflation jumped to 1.5% in August from 0.9% against a 1.0% forecast. Ofgem has confirmed the October price cap rises 3.6% to 1,723 pounds on higher wholesale gas, and UK gas is 172.07 GBp/therm, up 4.40% today and 22.02% on the month. That is the administered-energy channel that produced July's CPI reopening for the fourth quarter. GBP nonetheless STAYS at zero, because the other half of the picture is genuinely soft - core CPI flat at 2.6% for a third month, wage growth down to 4.1% from 4.4%, employment change halved to +83,000, retail sales -0.5% and Nationwide house prices missing at +1.6% y/y - and TE's own gilt commentary notes that a subdued labour market may make the Bank more cautious. The score is right; yesterday's reason for it was wrong, and that matters because EUR/GBP was built on it. That trade falls from HIGH to LOW-MED. The third change is the euro, downgraded from +2 to +1, and it comes from the national flashes rather than from anything the ECB said. Germany printed 2.9% for August, BELOW the 3.0-3.1% consensus, with core UNCHANGED at 2.4% and services inflation EASING to 2.8% from 2.9%; France came in at 2.4% with HICP 2.7%, but services slowed to 2.0% from 2.2%; and even Spain, which delivered the 4.3% headline the hawks wanted, saw core FALL to 2.9%. Every one of those moves is energy - German energy inflation 10.5% from 8.3%, French energy 16.7% from 12.6% - and none of it is the underlying pressure the Governing Council said it needed to see. On top of that German retail sales collapsed -3.4% m/m against a +0.4% forecast. The area-wide flash at 09:00Z carries a 3.3% consensus with core at 2.5%, and weighting Germany at 2.9% and French HICP at 2.7% against Spain does not get you to 3.3% - the risk into that print is a downside surprise, which is the opposite of what yesterday's file said. The ECB is still roughly 80% priced for a 2.50% deposit rate on September 10 and the euro is still a buy against the franc, but EUR/USD comes down to a RANGE into the number. The dollar holds at +1 rather than being upgraded again, and the restraint is deliberate. The pricing has genuinely extended - 65%-plus on FedWatch, the 10-year at 4.781% and the highest since January 2025, the 2-year at 4.356% - and the US services PMI jumped to 56.8 from 54.6. But Citi's Andrew Hollenhorst argues the speech was only marginally more hawkish than usual and that there was no consensus for a hike even in July, JPMorgan's David Kelly thinks the labour market deters the Fed, and TE's own summary of the July minutes warns the discussion predates data showing cooler employment and inflation. With payrolls Friday carrying a +55,000 consensus after a MINUS 23,000 print, moving the dollar two notches in two days would be exactly the whipsaw this file is supposed to avoid. Canada holds +1 with the growth story intact - Q2 at +3.3% annualised, the Q1 contraction revised away to +0.3%, business capex +2.3% - and gains a new forward leg: National Bank and Scotiabank now both forecast 50bp of BoC hikes by December, against Rabobank seeing nothing through 2027. All 35 economists polled expect a hold tomorrow at 13:45Z, so the statement language is the whole event, six days before C$27.6bn of retaliation lands. Australia holds +1 on the highest cash rate in the G10 at 4.35% and a trimmed mean stuck at 3.6%, and the China picture split rather than deteriorated: the NBS manufacturing PMI is 49.8 and contracting for a second month with non-manufacturing missing at 49.0, but the RatingDog private survey BEAT at 51.5 from 50.9. Net exports contributed +0.1% to Q2 GDP against a -0.4% forecast, which helps tomorrow's 01:30Z print where consensus is +0.3% q/q. New Zealand holds +1 into the RBNZ tomorrow at 02:00Z, but the track call needs balancing: yesterday leaned on ASB's 3.3% peak, and Westpac expects the Bank to be EQUIVOCAL about October and explicitly data-dependent with the OCR close to the 3% neutral rate, while the shadow board is split. Business confidence also fell to 53.7 from 56.1. The hike is priced; the track is genuinely two-sided. Switzerland stays at 0 and the franc failed a fourth test, with USD/CHF RISING to 0.80972 on a live exchange of fire. One factual fix: Swiss CPI is NOT today - it lands Thursday September 3 at 06:30Z, consensus 0.5% against 0.4% now. On geopolitics the tail cooled slightly even as the headlines stayed loud: Trump said the US would hit Iran hard but then told reporters the response would be NARROW, noting Iran's navy and air force are destroyed, and CENTCOM DENIED Tehran's claim that a supertanker was disabled by mines. UKMTO does report a tanker struck by three unknown projectiles near Khasab with no casualties. WTI is 86.463 and up 0.82%, Brent 91.19, and gold fell to 4,428.76, down 4.92% on the week but still up 9.21% on the month. The practical book is short: USD/CHF, EUR/CHF and CAD/CHF are the only clean one-notch legs, sell sterling against the dollar and the three commodity currencies, stay short gold in small size, and put nothing on ahead of a 09:00Z inflation print that consensus has probably set too high.

geopolitics: The war is in its seventh month and remains kinetic, but the tail cooled at the margin today even as the headlines stayed loud - and the distinction matters for how much risk premium to pay for. The escalation of record is unchanged: US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island on Sunday after the IRGC was observed preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the Strait, and Iran retaliated with a combined missile and drone operation against the US-operated King Hussein and Al Azraq air bases in Jordan, eight of which Jordan intercepted, plus a base in the UAE. Three things have changed since yesterday's file. First, Trump followed his vow to hit Iran hard by telling reporters at the White House that the military response would be NARROW, noting that many of Iran's leaders have been killed and that its navy and air force have been destroyed - which is a ceiling on the retaliation, not an opening. Second, CENTCOM has DENIED Tehran's claim that a supertanker was disabled by mines on the southern Hormuz route, a claim this file carried yesterday as unconfirmed and which should now be treated as false. Third, what did happen is smaller but real: UKMTO reports a tanker struck by three unknown projectiles while completing an outbound transit near Khasab, Oman, with no casualties and no environmental impact. Energy accordingly firmed rather than spiked: WTI is 86.463 and up 0.82% on the day and 5.01% on the week, Brent 91.190, European TTF gas 69.91 EUR/MWh and up only 0.14% today though still 21.55% on the month, German gas 70.85 and German power 146.41 and up 6.19%, UK gas 172.07 GBp/therm and up 4.40% today and 22.02% on the month, coal 141.75 and up 7.79% on the week. Roughly 6-8 million barrels a day still transit the Strait, mainly from non-Iranian Gulf producers. The FX transmission is where the useful information sits, and it splits three ways. Canada is the clean beneficiary and holds +1, with the oil leg now sitting alongside a +3.3% annualised Q2, a revised-away recession and two banks forecasting 50bp of BoC hikes by December. The euro is the interesting case and it is the reason EUR was downgraded today: gas at a January-2023 high is exactly the channel the ECB keeps citing, and it duly produced Spain at 4.3%, German energy inflation at 10.5% and French energy at 16.7% - but German core was FLAT at 2.4%, German services EASED to 2.8%, French services slowed to 2.0% and Spanish core FELL to 2.9%, so the shock is showing up as a headline the Council has said it will look through rather than the underlying pressure it said it needs. The same shock is a euro-area terms-of-trade hit, visible in German retail sales at -3.4% and the DAX closing 1.2% lower on Monday with Siemens Energy down 5%. The UK is the third channel and it is now hawkish rather than neutral: the Ofgem cap rises 3.6% to 1,723 pounds in October explicitly because of Middle East wholesale gas, BRC shop-price inflation jumped to 1.5%, and the gilt is the G10's highest at 5.2077% - which is precisely why sterling is a two-sided MIXED and not the funding leg. But the most informative observation is again a negative one, and it is now four tests deep: gold fell to 4,428.76 and the franc WEAKENED to 0.80972 across two consecutive days of live military exchange between American and Iranian forces. The haven complex is not pricing the Strait at all. It is pricing US real rates and a Fed above 65% for September, with the 10-year at 4.781% and its highest since January 2025 - which is why the Fed still outranks every headline out of the Gulf on this board, why XAU stays a short and why the franc remains the funding currency of choice.
